title: Hip osteoarthritis and frailty: getting out of a chair more safely (UK)
meta_title: Hip Arthritis and Frailty: Getting Out of a Chair Safely

direct_answer: To get out of a chair more safely with hip osteoarthritis and frailty, use a firm chair with arms at the right height, shuffle forward, lean forward with your nose over your toes and push up through the armrests. Regular sit-to-stand practice builds the leg strength that makes it easier.

content:
Getting out of a chair is something most people do many times a day, so when hip osteoarthritis and frailty make it hard, it affects everything. The right chair, a simple technique and regular practice can make standing up safer and easier, and help you stay independent.

This guide explains how to stand up and sit down more safely, how to choose and adjust your chair, and how to build strength. Follow any plan your physiotherapist or occupational therapist has given you first.

Why standing up gets harder

Standing from a chair needs the hip to bend, then strong thigh and buttock muscles to push you up. Hip osteoarthritis can make bending painful and stiff, and frailty usually means weaker muscles and slower balance reactions. Low, soft chairs make it harder still. Many people start to rock or pull on furniture, which can lead to falls.

How to stand up

  • Shuffle forward to the front of the seat.
  • Place your feet flat on the floor, slightly apart and a little behind your knees. If one hip is more painful, you can put that foot slightly forward.
  • Put your hands on the armrests.
  • Lean forward so your nose is over your toes.
  • Push up through your arms and legs together, then straighten up.
  • Stand still for a few seconds to check your balance before you walk. Reach for your walking aid only once you are standing steadily.

How to sit down

  • Walk right up to the chair and turn until you feel it against the back of your legs.
  • Reach back for both armrests.
  • Lean forward slightly and lower yourself slowly, rather than dropping into the seat.

Choosing and adjusting your chair

  • Firm seats with armrests are easiest. Avoid deep, soft sofas and low chairs.
  • When seated, your hips should be level with or slightly higher than your knees, with your feet flat on the floor.
  • Chair raisers, a firm cushion or a higher chair can help. An occupational therapist can measure you and advise.
  • Riser-recliner chairs can help some people, but they are expensive and can reduce leg practice. Ask for advice before buying.

Low sofas and other people's chairs

Sofas and chairs away from home are often lower and softer. Choose the firmest seat with arms, sit near the edge, and avoid sitting for long periods when you are stiff. If you get stuck, do not let others pull you up by your arms; ask them to steady the chair instead.

Building strength with sit-to-stand practice

Strength and balance exercise has good evidence for reducing falls, and NICE recommends exercise for osteoarthritis. Practising sit-to-stand a few times a day, at a height you can manage safely, builds the muscles you need. Start with a higher seat and use your arms, then gradually lower the seat or use your arms less as you get stronger. Some ache is normal, but stop if a joint becomes hot, swollen or much more painful.

When to ask for help

An occupational therapist can assess your chair and recommend equipment. A physiotherapist can give you exercises. Ask your GP for a referral, or contact your council for a free care needs assessment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 after a fall if you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or cannot get up.
  • Get urgent advice the same day if you suddenly cannot put weight on your leg, or have a hot, swollen joint with a fever.
  • See your GP if standing up is getting harder week by week, if you feel dizzy when you stand, or if you have had a fall.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it cheating to use a higher chair?

No. A seat at the right height lets your muscles work safely. You can lower it gradually as you get stronger.

Should I rock to get up?

A small forward lean is helpful. Large rocking movements can unbalance you; practise the technique above instead.

Can I get chair raisers free?

Often, after an occupational therapy assessment. Ask your GP or council.
